blocks.text: A Segment Tree is a binary tree built over an array where each node stores the answer, for example the sum, minimum, maximum, or gcd, for a specific contiguous range of that array. Internal nodes combine the answers of their two children, so any range answer can be assembled from a small number of precomputed pieces.

It is the natural, more general sibling of the Fenwick Tree. Where a Fenwick Tree is a compact trick that only works for invertible operations like sum and XOR, a Segment Tree works for any associative operation, including min, max, and gcd, and it can also apply updates to an entire range at once, not just a single element.
With a Segment Tree, all of the following run in O(log n) time:

items: Point Update: Change a single arr[i]
Range Query: Combine the answer over any range [l, r]
Range Update: Apply a change to every element in a range [l, r] at once, using lazy propagation

blocks.text: This makes it the default choice whenever a problem needs range queries with an operation that is not simple addition, or whenever it needs range updates rather than point updates.

content.title: 1. Why Fenwick Tree Is Not Enough

blocks.text: The Fenwick Tree is small, fast, and easy to code, but it has two hard limits.

items: It only supports invertible operations. Fenwick Tree range queries work by subtracting one prefix answer from another, rangeQuery(l, r) = query(r)-query(l-1). That subtraction only makes sense for operations that have an inverse, like sum and XOR. There is no way to undo a min or a max, so Fenwick Tree cannot answer range minimum or range maximum queries.

It does not support efficient range updates. Fenwick Tree can fake a range update for a point query using the difference array trick, but a true range update combined with a range query needs two Fenwick Trees and a careful formula, and even then it only works for sum.

blocks.text: A Segment Tree removes both limits. Because every node explicitly stores the combined answer of its children rather than relying on a reversible prefix trick, it works for any associative operation: sum, min, max, gcd, product under a modulus, bitwise AND or OR, and more.
It also supports genuine range updates through a technique called lazy propagation, covered later in this doc.

Rule of thumb: reach for Fenwick Tree when the operation is invertible, sum or XOR, and updates are point updates. Reach for Segment Tree when the operation is not invertible, min, max, or gcd, or when the problem needs range updates.

content.title: 2. The Core Idea: A Tree of Ranges

blocks.text: A Segment Tree is built by repeatedly splitting the array in half. The root represents the entire array range [0, n-1]. Its left child represents the left half of that range, and its right child represents the right half. Each of those children is split again, and again, until a node represents a single element, a leaf.
Every internal node's value is simply its left child's value combined with its right child's value, using whatever operation the tree is built for.

items: For a sum tree: tree[node] = tree[left] + tree[right]
For a min tree: tree[node] = min(tree[left], tree[right])
For a max tree: tree[node] = max(tree[left], tree[right])
For a gcd tree: tree[node] = gcd(tree[left], tree[right])

blocks.text: This is the entire idea. A Segment Tree is a precomputed hierarchy of overlapping answers, small enough to fit in O(n) space, that lets any range be reconstructed from at most O(log n) of its nodes.
Picture a tiny array of four elements, a = [2, 4, 5, 7], at indices 0 through 3, built as a sum tree.

blocks.caption: Each node stores the sum of its range. Leaves hold single elements. Internal nodes hold the sum of their two children.
blocks.text: /engineering/dsa-media/1785406762810-311645681.png

The root covers [0, 3] and stores 18, the sum of the whole array. It splits at the midpoint into [0, 1] and [2, 3], each storing the sum of its half. Those split again into the four leaves, each holding one raw element.
Two properties fall directly out of this construction:

items: Depth is O(log n). Because the range halves at every level, a tree over n elements has at most about log2(n) + 1 levels.
Total nodes is O(n). A tree over n leaves has fewer than 2n nodes in total, since it is very close to a full binary tree.

blocks.text: Segment Trees are almost always implemented on top of a plain array, not real pointer based tree nodes. The array is 1-indexed at the node level (a separate indexing system from the 0-indexed data range the tree stores):

items: The root lives at tree[1]
A node at index i has its left child at tree[2 * i]
A node at index i has its right child at tree[2 * i + 1]

blocks.caption: Node i's children live at 2i and 2i+1. Moving to a child just doubles the index, no pointers required.
blocks.text: /engineering/dsa-media/1785406762810-234649546.png
This mirrors the classic binary heap layout, and for the same reason: doubling and halving an integer index is far cheaper than following pointers, and it needs no extra memory for child links.
How much space does the array need?

For an array of n elements, this array based tree needs up to 4n slots. That bound is not tight, it comes from the tree not always being perfectly balanced when n is not a power of two, so the standard safe allocation is vector<long long> tree(4 * n).

Do not try to compute the exact node count and allocate precisely. Allocating 4n is the accepted convention, it wastes a small constant amount of memory but guarantees no out of bounds access for any n.

Building starts at the root with the full range [0, n-1] and recurses down. A leaf, where lo == hi, simply copies the raw array value. Every internal node waits for both of its children to finish, then combines them on the way back up.
Every node is visited exactly once, so build runs in O(n) total, even though it looks recursive and tree shaped.
Updating arr[idx] walks a single path from the root down to the leaf at idx, then recombines every ancestor on the way back up. Only one child is ever visited at each level, unlike range query.
The recombine step at the end matters even though only one child actually changed, the parent's stored value has to reflect both children's current values, not just the one that was touched.

content.title: 7. Range Query: the Three Way Branch

blocks.text: Every recursive call to query is handed a node that owns a range [lo, hi], and a target query range [l, r]. Exactly one of three situations is true, and the entire algorithm is just handling each of them correctly.

items: No overlap. The node's range and the query range do not intersect at all, r < lo or hi < l. This node contributes nothing, return the identity value for the operation (0 for sum, positive infinity for min) and stop.

Full overlap. The node's entire range sits inside the query range, l <= lo and hi <= r. The precomputed value at this node is already exactly the answer for this whole range, return tree[node] directly and stop. There is no need to look at its children at all.
Partial overlap. Neither of the above, the ranges overlap but neither contains the other. Split the range at the midpoint, recurse into both children, and combine their two answers.

blocks.caption: The three cases a query call can land in: skip a node entirely, use it directly, or split and recurse.
blocks.text: /engineering/dsa-media/1785406762987-367364547.png
blocks.alt: Range Query: the Three Way Branch

blocks.text: The partial overlap case is why range query is O(log n) and not O(n). Recursion only descends into subtrees that genuinely need splitting, most of the tree gets pruned away by the no overlap and full overlap checks before it is ever visited.

items: Build: O(n), every node is visited exactly once
Point update: O(log n), a single root to leaf path
Range query: O(log n) amortized, even though it can branch into two recursive calls at every level
Space: O(n), typically allocated as 4n to stay safe for any n

blocks.text: Why range query is still O(log n)
It looks like a function that branches in two at every level should cost O(n). It does not, because most of those branches terminate immediately in the no overlap or full overlap case.

A query range only forces real recursion along the two boundaries where it cuts through a node's range, one boundary on the left edge of the query and one on the right edge. Each boundary is a single root to leaf path of length O(log n), and everything else along the way resolves in one step.
Add those two boundary paths together and the total work is still O(log n), not O(log n) squared, since both paths are walked in the same single traversal rather than one after another.

content.title: 9. Worked Example: Tracing a Range Sum Query

blocks.text: Take the same four element array from earlier, a = [2, 4, 5, 7], and trace a call to query(1, 0, 3, 1, 3), the sum of indices 1 through 3.

blocks.caption: Nodes actually visited while answering sum(1, 3). The bottom left leaf is skipped entirely, and the right subtree is used directly without recursing further.
blocks.text: /engineering/dsa-media/1785406762988-903290811.png
blocks.alt: Worked Example: Tracing a Range Sum Query

codes.javascript:
query(node=1, range=[0,3], target=[1,3])
  [0,3] is neither disjoint from [1,3] nor fully inside it -> partial overlap, recurse
  mid = 1

  left  = query(node=2, range=[0,1], target=[1,3])
    [0,1] is neither disjoint nor fully inside [1,3] -> partial overlap, recurse
    mid = 0
    left  = query(node=4, range=[0,0], target=[1,3])
      [0,0] ends before [1,3] begins -> no overlap, return 0
    right = query(node=5, range=[1,1], target=[1,3])
      [1,1] sits fully inside [1,3] -> full overlap, return tree[5] = 4
    combine: 0 + 4 = 4

  right = query(node=3, range=[2,3], target=[1,3])
    [2,3] sits fully inside [1,3] -> full overlap, return tree[3] = 12 directly

  combine: 4 + 12 = 16

blocks.text: Only five nodes were touched out of the seven in the whole tree, and node 3 answered with a single lookup because its entire range already sat inside the query range. That single lookup, instead of two more recursive calls down to its leaves, is exactly what the full overlap case buys.

A point update touches one root to leaf path, O(log n) nodes. A naive range update, add a value to every element in [l, r], looks like it should cost O(n) in the worst case, since the recursion could be forced to touch every leaf underneath a partially overlapping node.

Lazy propagation avoids that by deferring work. When an update fully covers a node's range, instead of recursing all the way down to update every leaf underneath it, the node updates its own stored value immediately, and stores a note to itself, a lazy value, saying its children still owe this update. The update stops right there.

That deferred note only gets resolved, pushed down to the two children, the next time some other operation actually needs to visit those children, whether that is a future update or a future query. Until then the children's stored values are technically stale, but nothing has asked to see them yet, so it does not matter.

blocks.caption: A range add stops at a fully covered node and leaves a lazy marker. Children only get updated once something actually needs to visit them.
blocks.text: /engineering/dsa-media/1785406762988-518839984.png

The key discipline of lazy propagation: any function that is about to recurse into a node's children must first resolve that node's pending lazy value by calling pushDown. Forgetting this single call is the most common lazy propagation bug, covered again in Common Mistakes below.

With this deferral, both range update and range query become O(log n) again, the same bound as a point update, because a lazy value at any node is only ever pushed one level down at a time, and each operation only walks O(log n) root to leaf paths.
A lazy segment tree keeps a second array, lazy, parallel to tree. A nonzero lazy[node] means this node's own value is already correct, but its children have not been told about a pending change yet.

pushDown moves a node's pending lazy value one level down. Each child absorbs the update into its own stored value, scaled by how many elements that child actually covers, mid-lo+1 for the left child and hi-mid for the right child, and then remembers the same lazy value for its own future children. The parent's lazy value is cleared once this is done.

Notice that both updateRange and query call pushDown before recursing into children, exactly the discipline described above. Skipping that call in either function is enough to make the whole tree quietly return stale answers.

items: Sum segment tree: the standard form used throughout this doc. Combine is addition, identity is 0.
Min or max segment tree: combine is min or max. The identity must change too, positive infinity for min, negative infinity for max, never 0.
Segment tree with lazy propagation: adds true range update support on top of any of the above, covered in the previous two sections.

Merge sort tree: each node stores a sorted copy of its range instead of a single number, built the same way merge sort combines two sorted halves. Answers questions like counting how many elements in a range are less than some value, in roughly O(log squared n).

Persistent segment tree: an advanced variant where every update creates a new version of the tree while reusing all the unchanged nodes from the previous version, letting queries be answered against any historical version. Not covered in depth here, but worth knowing it exists for problems that ask about the state of an array at some earlier point in time.

These are the LeetCode style problems that most directly exercise a Segment Tree, several of them are the same problems Fenwick Tree solves, which makes them a good way to compare both structures on identical inputs.

items: Medium Range Sum Query, Mutable (LC 307): the same problem Fenwick Tree solves, useful for comparing both approaches side by side
Hard Range Sum Query 2D, Mutable (LC 308): extend the recursive structure to two dimensions, or nest a segment tree of segment trees
Hard Count of Smaller Numbers After Self (LC 315): a merge sort tree, or a segment tree over compressed ranks, counting smaller elements to the right
Hard Falling Squares (LC 699): a segment tree with lazy propagation over compressed coordinates, tracking a running maximum height
Hard My Calendar III (LC 732): a segment tree with lazy propagation for range add plus range maximum, to find the largest number of overlapping bookings

blocks.text: Most Segment Tree bugs trace back to one of a small handful of recurring mistakes.

items: Off-by-one errors in range boundaries. This implementation uses inclusive endpoints everywhere, [lo, hi] and [l, r] both include their right edge. Mixing an inclusive convention in one function with an exclusive convention in another is the single most common source of silently wrong answers.

Forgetting to push down a lazy value before recursing into a node's children. Any function, update or query, that is about to look at 2 * node or 2 * node + 1 must resolve that node's lazy value first, otherwise the children are read or written using stale data.

Using the wrong identity value for the operation. 0 is the identity for sum, but it is the worst possible identity for min, a real minimum can easily be larger than 0, but it is never larger than positive infinity. Match the identity to the operation, not the other way around.

Confusing the node array index with the data index. tree[i] refers to the i-th node in the 1-indexed node array, not the i-th element of the original array. Passing a raw data index where a node index was expected is a common transcription bug.

Recombining after only one recursive call instead of both. Update and query both need tree[2 * node] + tree[2 * node + 1] on the way back up, even a point update, which only walks one branch of the recursion, still has to recombine using both children's current values.
Under allocating the tree array. 4n is the safe convention, allocating exactly 2n or a tight power of two bound can silently write out of bounds for array sizes that are not themselves powers of two.

blocks.text: Neither structure replaces the other, they solve overlapping but distinct problems. If Fenwick Tree can express the operation cleanly, its smaller code and lower constant factor usually make it the better choice in an interview. Reach for Segment Tree the moment the operation is not invertible, or the problem asks for a genuine range update rather than a point update.

items: Can you implement build, point update, and range query from scratch, with correct base cases, in under ten minutes?
Can you explain the three cases inside query, no overlap, full overlap, and partial overlap, and why each one is necessary for correctness?
Do you know why range query is O(log n) even though it can make two recursive calls at every level?
Can you explain what a lazy value represents, and why pushDown must run before any recursion into children?
Do you know which identity value to use for the operation you are combining, 0 for sum, positive infinity for min, negative infinity for max?
Can you explain when Fenwick Tree is the better choice over Segment Tree, and when it is not even an option?
